analysis.one_liner: Gives workers and retirees stronger claims in business bankruptcies and caps executive bonuses.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in the final month of the 118th Congress, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a large company goes bankrupt, its executives often keep collecting bonuses while workers lose jobs, pensions, and promised benefits. This bill would rewrite the bankruptcy code to change that: it would roughly double the amount of back wages employees can recover ahead of other creditors, give workers and retirees direct claims when their pension or 401(k) holdings are wiped out, make it much harder for a company to tear up union contracts or cut retiree health benefits, and bar or claw back large executive bonus packages during bankruptcy. It never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and retirees of companies that file for bankruptcy: they would recover more back pay and severance, keep stronger claims to pension and 401(k) losses, get a seat at the table before union contracts or retiree benefits can be cut, and share in savings from limits on executive bonuses. Unions gain new standing to file claims and enforce agreements.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages and benefit-plan contributions from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and removes the 180-day lookback limit, so workers get paid ahead of ordinary creditors up to a higher amount.

Allows employees and retirees to claim the shortfall when their pension plan is terminated or the value of company stock in their 401(k) is lost through fraud or a breach of duty, and makes severance pay and unpaid benefit contributions payable administrative expenses.

Rewrites the rules for rejecting union contracts: a company must negotiate in good faith from a business plan, bear its own labor fees, meet a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard, and cannot get court approval to cut wages while paying insiders bonuses.
Requires courts weighing a company sale to give substantial weight to which buyer will preserve jobs, keep pay and conditions, and assume pension and retiree health obligations.

Bars most exit bonuses and incentive pay for insiders, senior executives, and the highest-paid employees unless part of a plan broadly available to all workers; caps executive retention pay at far lower levels than current law and requires court approval at no more than the 50th percentile of comparable-industry pay.

Creates clawback mechanisms: if a company cuts union wages or retiree benefits, the estate can recover a proportional share of the compensation paid to directors and top officers in the prior year, and can unwind bonus-type transfers made within a year before bankruptcy.

Makes unpaid post-filing wages, vacation, and severance chargeable against the value of secured lenders' collateral, even if the lender had a contractual waiver, so banks can no longer contract around paying workers first.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives and board members of distressed companies (bonus caps, lower retention-pay limits, and clawbacks of compensation), secured lenders such as banks and hedge funds (they absorb unpaid wage costs out of collateral and lose their current contractual waivers), and private equity or asset buyers, who would have to outbid rivals on job and pension preservation to win court approval of a sale.

drawbacks.text: The wage and severance priorities and the change forcing secured lenders to absorb unpaid compensation would raise the cost of lending to financially shaky companies, which could mean less rescue financing and more outright liquidations in marginal cases.

The new barriers to rejecting collective bargaining agreements and the requirement that asset sales favor the bidder preserving jobs and pensions could keep unprofitable operations alive longer or complicate sales, risking outcomes where a company fails entirely and all jobs are lost rather than being restructured.

Treating severance as earned in full at layoff and allowing retiree-benefit claims could shift losses toward other creditors and shareholders, raising borrowing costs that are passed on to consumers and investors generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and retirees, the upside is concrete and large: bankruptcy currently ranks them near the bottom while executive bonus programs are routinely approved, and this bill reverses that ordering. The honest tradeoff is that some distressed companies would find reorganization or sale more expensive, and in edge cases a stricter bargaining-rejection process could contribute to a liquidation that costs jobs. The bill's own design anticipates this by tying union-contract cuts to a business plan and a minimum-necessity standard, but the lender-facing provisions carry real credit-supply risk that the bill does not offset.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in the final month of the 118th Congress and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on December 5, 2024, joined by eight original cosponsors, including Republican Senator Josh Hawley, making the sponsorship bipartisan from the start.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was taken: the committee held no markup or hearing, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of distressed companies, secured lenders, and asset buyers are better off because the bill died: the existing bankruptcy rules that rank workers' claims low and allow generous insider bonus programs remain in place unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats except Senator Hawley of Illinois' neighboring Missouri, so sponsorship was bipartisan but thin, and no recorded opponent ever had to vote because the bill never left committee.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and board members of distressed companies
industries.note: The bill would cap and in many cases bar bankruptcy-period bonuses and exit pay for insiders and top officers, and let the estate claw back a share of prior-year compensation when union or retiree benefits are cut. Their gain under the status quo comes directly out of the recovery available to workers and retirees.

Unpaid post-filing wages and benefit contributions would be charged against their collateral, and lenders could no longer waive that obligation by contract. This closes one of the main ways lender recoveries currently outrank employee pay.

Courts would have to favor bidders that preserve jobs and assume pension and retiree health obligations, and bonus-type transfers made in anticipation of bankruptcy would be recoverable. Buyer strategies built on shedding labor obligations would become harder.

Unions could file proofs of claim, get company-paid fees in contract-rejection fights, keep grievance arbitrations alive through bankruptcy, and presumptively have settlement plans preferred in confirmation.
Withdrawal liability would be measured to include benefits accrued while the company was in bankruptcy, protecting pension funds that cover union workers.
